title: Causally Evaluating the Learnability of Formal Language Tasks
claim: A mixed task distribution hides which sub-task is harder, because a skewed mixing weight can make the easy part look hard.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right automaton diagram, branching from central start state
description: A single probabilistic finite-state automaton drawn as a horizontal graph with gray circles and black arrows. The start state q_ι sits in the center, marked by a downward arrow. A left branch labeled a/η leads to a double-circled accepting state REP, which has a self-loop labeled a/0.9. This is the star-free part of the language. A right branch labeled b/(1−η) leads to the accepting state ODD. ODD has a self-loop a/0.45 and exchanges b/0.45 and b/0.5 transitions with the non-accepting state EVEN, which has its own a/0.5 self-loop. This right side is the parity part. Edge labels use sans-serif letters with probabilities in math font. The eye goes first to the central start state and the η and 1−η branch weights. The top self-loop labels are slightly cropped.
caption: A \pfsaAcr recognizing the language $\symba\kleene{\symba} \cup \symbb \kleene{\symba} \kleene{(\symbb\kleene{\symba}\symbb\kleene{\symba})}$. The transitions left of $\qinit$ correspond to the star-free language ${\symba\kleene{\symba}}$ (which is easier for transformers to learn), and the ones to the right correspond to the \parity language (which is harder for transformers to learn). If $\eta \in [0, 1]$ is low, we might wrongly assume that ${\symba\kleene{\symba}}$ is harder to learn.
abstract: Language models, as multi-task learners, acquire a wide range of abilities during training. A fundamental question is how much task-specific data is needed to learn a given task. Answering this for natural language is difficult: tasks are hard to delineate and can confound one another. To rigorously investigate the relationship between data frequency and learnability, we turn to a controlled setting using formal languages induced from probabilistic finite automata. These serve as a methodological testbed to demonstrate that standard correlational evaluation practices are inherently flawed. To enable causal analysis, we introduce the binning semiring, an algebraic object that lets us control how often a targeted property occurs in a sampled corpus. We formulate the experimental pipeline as a causal graphical model and derive decomposed Kullback-Leibler divergence metrics to measure the learnability of specific sub-tasks. Our experiments show that evaluating learnability without causal intervention leads to incorrect conclusions due to confounders in correlational analysis, and serve as a warning about correlational pitfalls in natural-language settings.
